author: ACG
title: National Climate Change Demo in Dublin
content:
The annual Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI) has been issued. This is a tool used to see how well 64 countries (those which produce 90% of global greenhouse gas emissions) are doing at mitigating the worst aspects of climate change.




Obviously some places are doing better than others. Ireland is one country that is performing worse than the last time conditions were evaluated. There are complexities in the details, as with any real-world situation. Nevertheless, there are some bottom-line problems that are impossible to ignore.




The report says: “Despite superficially strong frameworks, the CCPI country experts note that progress on climate action is nowhere near sufficient…” It also states clearly “The experts criticise the lack of implementation of existing legislation, frequent introduction of exclusions, and limited understanding of the severity of the situation.” (https://ccpi.org/country/irl/).#




oplus_0




One of the major culprits in preventing progress is data centres. Here “The experts stress that progress in renewables deployment is falling behind surging energy demand. Data centres are the main driver, as they accounted for 23% of total electricity supply in 2025 and now exceed the demand of all households in Ireland. To meet the rising demand, the government has continued to support and even expand fossil fuel use instead of reducing dependence on imports.” (ibid)




So you have a country where the government talks the talk but in reality fails to keep its commitments and prefers to cosy up with big businesses that harm the environment. There should be no huge surprise in that. The experts who composed the CCPI report are hardly radicals and their work on the subject doesn’t exist in isolation. It is an international phenomenon that can be replicated to varying degrees across the world. The data speaks for itself and the idea that powerful people look after their own interests above everyone elses is something a lot of folks recognise.




Evidence of this recognition came in Dublin, with a 5,000-strong National Climate Demo on November 14th, pre-dating the CCPI report by 4 days. In many ways the gathering was unremarkable. That’s certainly the case




in terms of the scheduling and route of the march. It took about an hour and went through the CBD and ended near the government buildings.




Oplus_131072




As with other recent demonstrations, the most impressive aspect of the action was the sheer range of people who participated. You could just about tick off an entire alphabetical bingo card of groups and individuals who joined. Everyone from anarchists to doctors, environmentalists to Palestinian protestors, Quakers to socialists and vegans. Those involved were aware of the seriousness of the issue, but there was a vibrancy to the march that manifested more as a colourful concern than a militant anger. That is probably to be expected in such a disparate crowd.




Its risky to assume too much, but given the overall tone of the demo, its likely many who joined would have favoured an approach similar to the writers of the CCPI report. Its an outlook characterised by recognition of a critical problem but calls on politicians to do this and that to ensure its resolution. For those of us with a more radical perspective, such demonstrations are an opportunity to initiate discussions and exchanges on why the latter view is faulty and to suggest alternatives.




It is probably fair to say environmental consciousness is currently high among the population at large, and especially so for those who actively join campaign groups and demos. The challenge is therefore not so much making people aware of the problem of climate change, as introducing them to ways of thinking or theories and methods they might not be familiar with.




Anarchists were approached during the November 14th action by fellow participants. The majority seemed curious about who we are and what we stand for. There used to be an active anarchist movement in Ireland from the 80s through to a few years ago (https://libcom.org/article/workers-solidarity-movement-closing-statement). Its not easy to maintain organisations and activity across time, and things are at a bit of a low ebb now. It has resulted in a bunch of folks (not always based on their generation or age) who aren’t familiar with anarchism or our organisations. It’s a shame, but we have to begin from how things are on the ground, not how we wish them to be.




oplus_32




On the upside, the dearth of knowledge provides fresh opportunities to put our views across. During discussions on the climate demo, there was often common agreement about the nature of the environmental crisis but pleasant surprise when people had dialogues with us about possible solutions they hadn’t be aware of. Some contacts were initiated and ideas considered.




We need reliable information. We also need to be a pole of attraction for the many people who already have information but are stuck in dead-end approaches to using it. The experience of the National Climate Demo in Ireland shows in its own way, that some progress can be made in doing so.

title: Against Labour’s Militarism: No War but the Class War
content:
The recent Budget told us which priorities Labour were setting. Billions for war, and slashing funding in other areas of spending. Arms manufacturers will receive greater government backing, and the development and manufacture of military technology will be a growing part of industrial strategy.




Chancellor Healey will be spending “£10bn of additional economic and military support—based on loans, Export Finance guarantees, and half a billion in urgent military funding for this winter.”. This is in addition to the £25 billion already put into defence by previous Tory and Labour governments. As the Budget pledged, “the government’s fully funded Defence Investment Plan will deliver stronger front-line military capability, supporting jobs, businesses and economic growth across the UK.” There will be £5 billion for advanced uncrewed systems for the rest of this Parliament, up to 2030. This includes £300 million for the StormFighter combat-air programme and £400 million for Army drone technology.




All this will mean an additional £15 billion annually on the military (rising to £36 billion a year if long term targets are met).




One of the events that triggered Starmer’s leaving of the scene, was the resignation of Healey as defence secretary.  He left because he felt that defence spending fell“well short of what is required for defence and the country at this dangerous time”. He talked about the invasion of Ukraine and the Russian threat, and talked about a Russian attack predicted by NATO by 2030. Now, three weeks after his initial resignation, Healey is Chancellor, and imposing his defence plans.




The government has re-affirmed its obligations to NATO to spend 3% of GDP by 2030, and 3.5% by 2035, the details of which will not be published until the 2027 spending review.  In addition, the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank will put up to £5 billion over four years into defence, dual-use technologies and related national security sectors. The Innovative Defence Financing Taskforce has been established to seek additional private and international capital.




In order to pay for all this defence spending, this would be done by slashing the budgets of other departments by 1% from 2027‑28 to 2029‑30 to raise £3 billion, with £1.7 billion from the Treasury’s capital reserve.  One of the projects that will suffer is the Warm Homes Plan, which will get a cut of £1 billion. This comes at a time when many are facing higher energy bills. As was noted in the Budget statement, “… it is not necessarily the case that all departments will see real-terms increases at the next spending review”




The money is hard to find. Labour is too timid to put taxes on the rich. Already, thanks to years of austerity cuts from both Tories and Labour there is very little to spend. So what Labour will do, is attack benefits. In fact, Healey told the House of Commons after the Budget that “There will be a reduction in the benefits bill.”




This can be seen with the recent review entitled “Young People and Work” headed up by Alan Milburn, a Blairite Labour MP. This threatens the taking away of sickness and disability benefits for under-25s. They would be barred from claiming Universal Credit or the Personal Independence Payment (PIP), the main disability benefit, and instead receive a new youth allowance.




Milburn supports schemes like Sainsbury’s Modern Work Experience Programme, also endorsed by Burnham, where the supermarket chain would use 10,000 young people as unpaid labour.  




Any under-25s who fail to engage with the scheme proposed by Milburn would risk losing part of the allowance. He received the full support of Andy Burnham on this, who is open about increasing military spending, paid for by cutting benefits.




Another ominous move by Labour is the forthcoming review of disability benefits by the disability minister, Stephen Timms, another Blairite, indicating further welfare benefit cuts.




This upping of military spending and cutting of welfare spending has been prepared for by the right- wing press and think tanks. The notorious Paul Johnson called for Burnham to cut PIP, whilst talk about abolishing the triple lock on state pensions is rife in right wing rags. Alongside this is rabid propagandising for increased military spending from the likes of the Daily Mail and the Daily Telegraph. In addition, the sick, the disabled and the young are increasingly targeted as scroungers.




Recently, the right-wing think tank Centre for Social Justice (CSJ), which was founded by former Tory leader Iain Duncan Smith, published 

State of Dependency

, arguing that the benefits system was dragging the UK down, and stating, among much else, that the “increase in welfare spending this year alone is equivalent to 15 advanced Royal Navy frigates, 220 fighter jets, or 250,000 soldiers’ salaries, more than three times the size of the regular British Army.” The CSJ clearly makes a distinction between “deserving” and “undeserving” poor, talking about “medicalised worklessness”, and clearly aiming at abolishing PIP.




For her part, the Tory leader Kemi Badenoch whined that the extra spending needed to reach the pledged 3 percent of GDP on military spending by 2030 was “less than a third of the increase in welfare since Labour came to office.”




The UK Strategic Defence Review of 2025, penned by NATO supporters and partisans of Trump, sketched a scenario where one of its contributors, Fiona Hill, said that “we’re already in a situation where you could describe this as World War III structurally”, a ludicrous statement bearing in mind Russia’s inability to gain victory over Ukraine. This has fed Healey’s talk about a Russian attack in 2030.




Hill went on to talk in the Guardian about the UK needing a “different mindset”, involving greater internal cohesion, in other words, total class peace and class collaboration. The Strategic Defence Review advocated a public outreach campaign with the Department for Education developing “understanding of the armed forces among young people” and an expansion of cadet forces in schools and communities. ‘Anchor partnerships’ must be built with “a small set of trusted universities” to develop military science and technology. To reverse the decline in forces numbers from a Cold War peak of 311,000 regular personnel – with the army today, at 73,790, its smallest since 1714 and facing “a longstanding recruitment and retention crisis” – the review talks hopefully of “a national conversation led by the government” that maybe could “reconnect defence with society”.




Last month Burnham promised every young person a “high-quality technical pathway, work placements, apprenticeships and the skills and experience they need to secure a good job,” with “timely, high-quality mental health support”. This is offered in place of a university education that tuition fees and the rising cost of living are putting ever further out of reach, leaving it increasingly a route open only to the children of the wealthy.




Who gains most from all of this? The UK arms industry. BAE Systems, Britain’s largest defence contractor, saw its shares rise by 7.81% over the previous five days before the Budget, reaching £20.85 by late morning on 29th October 2026. It is the arms manufacturers who profit greatly from the current war fever.




All of this is not just a British phenomenon. Germany is looking towards increasing its military spending whilst cutting benefits, and there is a similar situation in France.  Pay, pensions, and public services are also under attack at the expense of defence spending.  Whilst the protests shaking Europe do not address this as a central concern, it is increasingly being brought to the attention of those involved in these movements.




We do not think that a Labour government with a “left” agenda would be any different. We have seen Corbyn’s capitulation to NATO when he was Labour leader. Corbyn has a long record of supporting anti-militarist and nuclear disarmament initiatives. The Manifesto produced by Labour at the time stated that a “Labour government will undertake a Strategic Defence and Security Review to assess the security challenges facing Britain, including new forms of hybrid, cyber and remote warfare.” It said that at least 2% of Gross Domestic Product would be spent on defence and that Labour would contribute £100 million to UN operations.




Having a ‘better’ leader, a more ‘radical’ programme, or more favourable circumstances will not make any difference next time. The ruling class will do everything in its power to ensure that the rule of capital continues on their terms.

author: ACG
title: When Anarchism Ceases to Be Anarchist: Liberalism, Subjectivism and the Loss of the Revolutionary Horizon
content:
Below is the second of two texts produced by Spanish libertarian writers., this time from a member of the Spanish anarchist organisation Liza, based in  Granada and Madrid. We reproduce these texts, not because we necessarily agree 100 per cent with their arguments, but because they make valuable and stimulating arguments, necessary for the strengthening and development of anarchist  communism.




There is a discussion within anarchism that for too long has been relegated to the background. It is not a question of determining who possesses an anarchist certificate of authenticity or of establishing a doctrinal orthodoxy. It is a question of examining what conception of society, freedom, power, conflict and social transformation really sustains a given position and what political consequences follow from it.




Table of Contents




Anarchism is not only a negation of the state, an abstract defence of individual freedom, a cultural sensibility, or a collection of horizontal practices. In the anarchist tradition, emancipation implies transforming the social relations of domination and developing forms of self-management capable of replacing them through a revolutionary process. Felipe Corrêa has synthesised this conception through three articulated elements: revolution, critique of domination and defence of self-management.




This definition allows us to establish a fundamental starting point. Anarchism cannot be defined only by what it rejects. Its specificity also lies in the social relations it seeks to build and in the forces capable of making them possible. The question is not only whether a position is anti-state, anti-capitalist or pro-freedom, but also to determine what it means by these concepts, what social relations it identifies as the foundation of domination and how it intends to transform them.




It is from this perspective that it becomes important to examine the liberal and subjectivist influences that run through certain sectors of contemporary anarchism. The problem is not the intellectual origin of each concept considered in isolation. This is what happens when certain categories modify the way in which society is understood to the point of displacing the analysis of social relations, organisation and revolution.




1. Liberalism does not necessarily enter through the front door




When one speaks of liberal influences within anarchism, the most immediate reaction is to seek an explicit defence of the market, private property, or the minimal state. That search can overlook much deeper forms of influence.




Luigi Fabbri already warned about the so-called “bourgeois influences” within anarchism. The problem was not necessarily that the anarchists affected by them consciously became defenders of the bourgeoisie. It consisted of the incorporation of categories produced by bourgeois society that could alter the understanding of organisation, solidarity, social struggle and revolution.




Liberal influence can operate, therefore, by preserving the libertarian vocabulary while transforming the categories through which reality is interpreted. Autonomy, freedom, resistance or emancipation can maintain a radical appearance while detached from the material relations that provide them with political content.




Displacement appears when the individual becomes the privileged unit of analysis, when autonomy is separated from collective organisation, when immediate resistance replaces strategy, or when subjective will begins to explain phenomena determined by historical relations. It also appears when identity displaces material positions, when personal transformation is presented as equivalent to social transformation, or when the critique of the State replaces the analysis of the relations of domination in which it is inserted.




It is not a question of affirming that every defence of individual autonomy is liberal. Nor is it a question of reducing anarchism to a sociology of classes. The question is different. The individual and the collective are not confronting realities. They are in a historical relationship of mutual constitution. The individual acts within social relations that he has not created and these relations can be reproduced or transformed through conscious and collective action.




Ideological filtering becomes problematic precisely when this relationship breaks down and one of its terms goes on to explain the other. When society appears as the result of autonomous individuals who subsequently relate, social structures cease to be the starting point of analysis. When, on the other hand, the collective becomes an abstraction placed above those who compose it, individual autonomy is also annulled. A coherent anarchist perspective needs to reject both reductions.




2. The problem of the abstract individual




Vladimir Benoit’s critique of the so-called “anarchist liberalism” is useful in specifying this problem. Its central concept is methodological individualism, understood as the tendency to take the isolated individual as a fundamental unit to explain society.




From this perspective, classes, organisations, unions, and social movements end up appearing as aggregates of individuals. Society is explained on the basis of the particular decisions of its members rather than on the basis of historical relations that determine the conditions under which those decisions can occur.




This does not imply denying the individual or his autonomy. Nor does it mean that every individualistic conception of freedom is necessarily liberal. The problem arises when the isolated individual becomes a sufficient explanation of phenomena that possess a relational existence.




Exploitation is not the sum of personal experiences of precariousness. Wage labor is not simply a choice repeated by millions of individuals. Property is not a private preference. The State cannot be understood as the cumulative result of particular administrative decisions. All these realities express historical relations that condition the action of individuals and that, at the same time, are reproduced or disputed through their activity.




Reversing this relationship has political consequences. A social structure can end up being translated into the language of individual experience. Exploitation becomes personal precariousness. Domination becomes interpersonal relationships. Organisation appears as a matter of preferences. Social conflict becomes a problem of conscience, identity or behaviour.




The result is an impoverished conception of politics. Society ceases to appear as a historical totality traversed by power relations and material antagonisms and begins to be conceived as the sum of particular experiences whose subsequent articulation would produce the collective.




The problem is not to recognise the individual dimension of oppression. The problem is to turn it into the fundamental explanation of relationships that exist before each individual and that require collective intervention to be transformed.




3. From social analysis to psychologism




When the individual occupies the centre of the analysis, the will inevitably acquires an increasing weight. If social phenomena are explained mainly by the decisions and dispositions of the subjects, politics ends up concentrating on what they do, think or represent.




From this arises a form of radicalism focused on the permanent evaluation of individual coherence. It examines whether a person is sufficiently autonomous, whether he or she reproduces authority, whether he or she maintains horizontal practices, whether he or she uses appropriate language or whether his or her interpersonal relationships reproduce certain forms of domination.




These issues can be politically relevant. The transformation of everyday relations and the critique of the forms of power that run through social life are part of the anarchist tradition. The problem begins when this level replaces the analysis of the social relations that make these behaviours possible.




A material perspective demands different questions. What relationships produce a certain situation? Who controls the resources and the means of production? How is exploitation reproduced? Which institutions guarantee its continuity? What social forces can confront it? What organisational capacity exists to intervene on it?




The difference is not merely methodological. A policy focused on subjective coherence tends to turn conflict into a moral issue. A policy oriented to the analysis of social relations seeks to identify forces, interests, structures and organisational capacities.




The will is indispensable for any conscious transformation, but it does not explain by itself the conditions under which it can act. Revolutionary consciousness does not exist outside of history. It is formed within certain social relations and acquires transformative capacity when it is articulated with a collective practice capable of intervening on them.




Emancipation therefore requires subjective transformation and social transformation. The former may contribute to the latter, but it cannot replace it.




4. When Anarchy Becomes an Ideal Type




There is another form of abstraction that operates in a seemingly opposite direction. It consists in converting a certain representation of “Anarchy” into the criterion by which every concrete practice is immediately judged.




In this case, anarchy ceases to function as a political horizon and set of guiding principles to become an idealised model against which organisations, demands and experiences are evaluated. That which does not coincide with the model appears to be insufficiently anarchist, while that which reproduces certain formal features can be elevated to an expression of anarchy.




The relationship between theory and reality is thus inverted. Instead of using principles to guide the analysis of concrete historical situations, an abstract image of the future is used to judge reality from outside its contradictions.




A revolutionary policy demands something different. A demand, an organisation or a collective experience must be analysed in terms of the social relations they express, the forces they mobilise, the interests they confront, the contradictions they contain and the possibilities they open.




This does not mean abandoning principles. On the contrary, principles are necessary precisely because they make it possible to determine the emancipatory meaning of a transformation and to distinguish anarchism from other forms of radicalism. What must be rejected is to turn them into a finished description of every historical experience.




The difference is decisive. Principles guide practice. The ideal type is intended to replace concrete analysis. The former allow us to intervene without losing sight of the revolutionary horizon. The second can turn anarchy into a morality external to history.




Anarchism does not need to find experiences that perfectly reproduce an imagined future society. It needs to understand existing conditions, intervene on their contradictions and develop the forces capable of transforming them.




5. Classes as social relations




This question appears with particular clarity in the conception of social classes. Formally recognising the existence of workers and capitalists is not enough. It is also necessary to understand what makes them class.




A class is not a statistical set of individuals who share income, professions, or economic characteristics. It is a historically determined social relation. The existence of the working class depends on certain relations of property, production, work and appropriation. The capitalist class occupies the corresponding position within these same relations.




The capitalist is not simply a wealthy individual. The worker is not simply someone who receives a salary. Both occupy social positions determined by a structure that conditions their possibilities of action and whose reproduction depends on concrete practices.




Therefore, the class struggle cannot be reduced to a psychological conflict between groups of individuals. Its foundation lies in objective social relations that produce differentiated positions within the reproduction of society. Individuals participate in them and can face them, but they do not produce them through their isolated decisions.




Nor does this imply reducing all domination to the economy. The state, gender, racism, culture, and ideology all have specific dynamics. A rigorous materialism does not consist in converting all contradictions into a mechanical reflection of the economy, but in situating them within the historical and material relations that condition its development.




The issue is the same again. Where the relational dimension disappears, structures can end up being interpreted as effects of individual consciousness. Social transformation is then subordinated to the modification of the attitudes of the subjects.




But a social relationship does not disappear because the subjective dispositions of those who participate in it change. It requires a transformation of the conditions that allow it to be reproduced.




6. Liberal freedom and anarchist freedom




The difference between the liberal and anarchist conceptions of freedom cannot be reduced to affirming that one defends freedom and the other seeks to expand it. Both traditions contain different positions, but there is a fundamental difference in the way of understanding the social conditions of freedom.




A liberal conception can understand freedom as the existence of a sphere of action protected against external interference, particularly against political power. The central problem is then to determine which restrictions must be eliminated in order to preserve individual decision-making capacity.




Anarchism introduces an additional question. It is not enough to ask what interference the individual is formally protected from. It is also necessary to ask under what material conditions he can effectively exercise his freedom.




Legal equality does not eliminate inequalities arising from property relations. A worker can be legally free and materially dependent on the sale of his labor power. He may enjoy the same formal rights as the owner of a company and yet lack equivalent capacity to decide on the conditions of production.




From an anarchist perspective, freedom cannot be separated from the social relations that allow it to be exercised. It does not only consist of having a private space in front of authority, but of participating in relationships where no one is subject to a separate power and where the conditions of existence can be decided collectively.




Freedom thus acquires a material and social dimension. It is not only a matter of limiting political power, but of transforming the relations that produce dependence and subordination. Hence the question of freedom leads directly to self-management.




7. Self-management, organisation and anti-statism




Self-management does not mean that each individual manages his or her own affairs in isolation. It means that those who participate in a social activity can collectively control the conditions in which it takes place.




That is why it presupposes organisation. Production, distribution, deliberation and collective life require coordination. The anarchist problem is not to eliminate any organisational structure, but to prevent coordination from becoming a separate body capable of imposing decisions on those who constitute it.




Autonomy and organisation are not, therefore, contradictory terms. An organisation can expand the effective capacity of individuals precisely because it allows the coordination of forces that would remain isolated without it. The decisive question is how functions are distributed, who controls decisions, how delegations are revoked and what mechanisms prevent the formation of a separate power.




Federalism expresses this logic at the level of articulation between different social units. It is not simply administrative decentralisation. It involves coordinating organisations and communities through structures subject to the control of those who constitute them. But neither can political decentralisation be reduced to a sufficient solution. Territorially distributing power does not in itself eliminate exploitation or transform property relations.




This explains why isolated anti-statism is not enough to define anarchist politics. Opposing the state can coexist with very different conceptions of property, the economy, and social organisation. Reducing state functions does not necessarily equate to abolishing the relations of domination that structure society.




The anarchist problem is not simply to determine how much power the state should have. It consists of transforming the social conditions that make possible the separation between those who govern and those who are governed.




Therefore, abolishing an institution without transforming the relations that reproduce domination can leave intact the conditions for it to reappear in another form. Anti-statism acquires its revolutionary meaning when it is articulated with the transformation of property relations, social equality, collective organisation and self-management.




Self-management thus constitutes the positive dimension of anti-statism. It responds not only to who should not govern, but to how the conditions of social life can be organised without producing a separate instance of power.




8. From Stirner to the Politics of Subjectivity




Max Stirner’s critique introduces a question that deserves to be treated more precisely. To reduce his thought to a simple radical liberalism would be insufficient. A central part of his work is to question the abstractions that acquire authority over the individual. The state, citizenship, morality, humanity, or “man” can become entities to which people must subordinate themselves.




This critique retains an obvious utility for anarchism. No collective category should be transformed into a sacred entity placed above those who constitute it. But it does not follow that every collective category is an illegitimate abstraction.




A class can express a real social relation without becoming a metaphysical essence. An organisation can perform a political function without becoming a sacred entity. A society can be the object of collective transformation without being elevated to a transcendent subject.




The problem is not in using collective categories, but in substantiating them and separating them from the concrete relations that provide them with content.




This question acquires special relevance in certain contemporary currents that have developed critiques of fixed identities, universal subjects and essentialist categories. There is no linear continuity between Stirner, Nietzsche, Foucault, Deleuze, Derrida and the so-called “post-anarchism”. However, certain theoretical concerns have acquired considerable influence in sectors of contemporary libertarian thought.




These tools can be productive when they question naturalised forms of power or rigid conceptions of subjects. The problem arises when the critique of identity becomes a critique of concrete social positions. The fact that an identity is not an immutable essence does not mean that the social relations associated with it lack reality. The fact that class is historically changing does not mean that class relations disappear. The fact that an organisation can produce power relations does not mean that all organisation is equivalent to domination.




Displacement becomes politically problematic when revolution comes to be conceived primarily as a transformation of subjectivity. Everyday resistance can then acquire a centrality that displaces stable organisation, strategy and structural transformation.




Here it is important to distinguish revolution and insurrection. An insurrection may imply a break with existing forms of subjectivity and authority. A revolution, on the other hand, also involves a transformation of social relations and institutions. Both dimensions can be part of the same process, but they are not equivalent.




Transforming subjectivity can contribute to an emancipatory practice. It cannot replace the transformation of relations that reproduce exploitation and domination.




The problem is not to recognise the importance of subjectivity or to deny that power runs through everyday relationships. It is to prevent this analysis from completely absorbing the terrain of revolutionary politics. A multiplicity of resistances can produce cultural and subjective changes without substantially modifying property, work, production or institutional forms of power.




The revolutionary question remains intact. What forces can transform existing relationships? What forms of organisation can articulate them, and what strategy can turn these dispersed capacities into a historical force?




9. From liberal filtration to the loss of the revolutionary horizon




Liberal influences can also be produced through the co-optation of the libertarian vocabulary itself. Shelagh Roxburgh’s research on 

so-called soft anarchism

 is illustrative in showing how concepts associated with anarchism can be incorporated into liberal frameworks, particularly in the theory of international relations.




Networks, decentralisation, cooperation, resistance, and non-state actors can be integrated into governance discourses without necessarily retaining their anti-capitalist content. The effectiveness of this co-optation lies precisely in the fact that it does not need to eliminate radical language. It can preserve words while modifying the conceptual relationships that gave them meaning.




Autonomy can be detached from ownership. Cooperation can be separated from exploitation. Resistance can be reduced to a permanent practice without a revolutionary horizon. Decentralisation can become an administrative technique. Participation can exist without effective control over resources.




Here Fabbri’s notion of “bourgeois leaks” becomes important again. Its usefulness lies not in classifying people as bourgeois or revolutionary, but in analysing how categories produced within bourgeois society can be incorporated into an emancipatory theory and modify its presuppositions.




Bourgeois society does not produce only certain economic relations. It also produces historical conceptions of the individual, freedom, property, competition, responsibility, and autonomy that can be presented as universal. When these categories organise political analysis, essentially social relations can end up being interpreted as individual problems.




The same displacement can affect the conception of class and organisation. If structures are translated into personal experiences, class ceases to appear as a social relation. If every organisation is treated primarily as a potential source of hierarchy, the need to build collective capacities can become a problem in itself.




The critique of rigid identities can serve to combat essentialisms. It does not justify, however, abandoning social relations as an object of analysis. Similarly, recognising that organisations can produce power does not imply that organising is tantamount to reproducing domination.




The result of these successive reductions can be a policy focused on local resistances, subjective practices and daily ruptures. Such experiences can be part of a revolutionary strategy. They become a substitute for revolution when they are no longer linked to the transformation of social relations.




The problem then reaches its clearest form. Revolutionary language can survive after that which made it revolutionary has disappeared. Autonomy, cooperation, participation, decentralisation and resistance can coexist with the existing order if they are separated from ownership, exploitation, social conflict and self-management.




The question is not whether certain practices are radical enough. It is whether they contribute to the development of the forces capable of transforming the social relations that produce domination.




10. Towards a social and revolutionary reconstruction of anarchism




Recovering the revolutionary horizon does not require building a closed doctrine. It requires the re-establishment of a coherent relationship between freedom, material conditions, social relations, organisation and collective capacity.




Anarchist freedom cannot be reduced to the absence of interference or to legal equality. Its exercise depends on specific conditions such as access to resources, time, education, decision-making capacity and control over living conditions. Therefore, emancipation requires transforming the relations that produce dependence, including the ownership of the means of production and the organisation of work.




Self-management expresses this transformation in positive terms. It does not mean simply participating in decisions, but collectively exercising control over the social conditions that determine one’s existence.




Nor can anti-statism constitute a separate program. Abolishing the State requires transforming the relations that make possible the separation between rulers and ruled, but also those that produce economic dependence and concentration of power. The question is not only which institution should disappear, but what social forms can make its existence unnecessary.




This places organisation at the centre of the revolutionary problem. Organisation does not mean authority by definition. What is decisive are the power relations it establishes, the mechanisms of control over its functions, the participation of its members and the possibility of revoking delegations. An organised structure can reproduce domination or expand the collective capacity of those who make it up.




Malatesta linked revolution to conscious action, organisation, and the creation of new social relations. The militants of 

Dyelo Truda

, starting from their interpretation of the Russian Revolution, also insisted on the problems arising from the absence of an anarchist organisation capable of coordinating a coherent revolutionary intervention. This does not make platformism a mandatory model. Its relevance lies in a more general question: a revolutionary force needs mechanisms capable of coordinating action without separating the political leadership from those who produce it.




The same perspective allows us to distinguish reform and reformism. A partial claim can improve living conditions and strengthen the organisation. It becomes reformism when it ceases to be part of a strategy of transformation and becomes the definitive horizon. Nor does the revolution need be reduced to a single insurrectionary moment. It can develop through a prolonged process of conflict, organisation, self-management, and social transformation, provided that the partial struggles maintain a conscious relationship with that horizon.




Murray Bookchin’s critique of 

so-called lifestyle anarchism

 is pertinent here, even if his opposition between “social anarchism” and “lifestyle anarchism” is too rigid to encompass the historical plurality of anarchism. Individual practices can contribute to an emancipatory culture, but they do not in themselves replace the transformation of social structures. The problem is not personal transformation. It is to make it the main terrain of revolutionary politics.




Defending a social perspective does not mean sacrificing the individual to an abstract collectivity. Individual and society are inseparable dimensions of human existence. Cooperation can expand individual freedom when it allows for collective control over material living conditions. Anarchist communism does not conceive of the community as a negation of individuality, but as a condition for its development without subordination.




The historical plurality of anarchism does not oblige relativism either. It is not necessary to construct a closed canon or to establish a definitive definition of anarchism. But recognising diversity does not mean considering all conceptions of freedom, domination, organisation, and revolution as equivalent. Different diagnoses produce different strategies.




The relevant criterion is not doctrinal purity, but coherence between the analysis of social relations, the emancipatory horizon and the means proposed to achieve it.




Contributions from other intellectual traditions can be incorporated critically. A revolutionary theory does not need to isolate itself intellectually. It needs to retain the capacity to subject any conceptual tool to its own emancipatory objectives and reject those categories that end up hiding the relations it seeks to transform.




The social and revolutionary reconstruction of anarchism therefore involves recovering a perspective capable of linking autonomy and collective capacity, freedom and material conditions, anti-statism and social transformation, concrete struggles and revolutionary strategy.




It is not a question of preserving a doctrinal identity in the face of all external influence. It is a matter of preventing concepts such as freedom, autonomy, resistance or participation from being separated from the social relations that provide them with political content.




The fundamental question remains open, but it is not ambiguous. What relations of domination must be abolished, what social forms can replace them and what collective capacity is necessary to make this transformation possible.




Don Diego de la Vega, militant of Liza.

title: The Proletariat and the Possibility of Revolution
content:
We re-publish below a text from the Spanish historian

 

Agustin Guillamón

, author of among other books, The Friends of Durruti Group 1937-1939 and  

Ready for Revolution

: 

The CNT Defense Committees in Barcelona, 1933-1938. This is the first of two interesting texts from Spanish writers that we will be putting up on the ACG website.




Introduction




The difference between Miquel Amorós and myself doesn’t lie in one wanting revolution and the other rejecting it, nor in one defending autonomy and the other not. We both start from a radical critique of capitalist society and the conviction that emancipation cannot be the work of institutions separate from those who struggle. We both reject the integration of struggles into state institutions and deeply distrust any organisation that seeks to replace direct worker action. However, when we try to define what this autonomy means, what relationship it should have with the transformation of society, and, above all, who can carry this transformation to its ultimate consequences, a fundamental difference emerges between us.




I would say that this difference can be formulated as follows: Amorós emphasises the concrete reconstruction of autonomous forms of life, while I consider it necessary to ask about the social subject capable of transforming these necessarily partial experiences into a general transformation of capitalist relations. This is not about denying the value of autonomous experiences, nor about postponing emancipation to an indefinite future. It is about determining what social force can transform what today appears as a limited experience into a general way of organising life. This question necessarily leads to the proletariat, and in it, in my view, lies the essential difference between our respective positions.




Amorós begins with a historical observation that cannot be ignored. The traditional forms of the workers’ movement have been profoundly weakened by the evolution of capitalism. Political representation, union integration, the fragmentation of labour, and the transformation of lifestyles have destroyed a good part of the conditions that allowed the proletariat to constitute itself, at certain historical moments, as a visible, organised revolutionary force capable of directly intervening in society. Faced with this situation, passively awaiting a future revolutionary recomposition would be a form of impotence. If emancipation has any real content, it must begin in the present.




Hence the importance that autonomy, community, and concrete utopia acquire in Amorós’s work. Revolution cannot be a promise that indefinitely justifies the acceptance of a subjugated life. We must reclaim now the capacities that capitalism has taken from us: To decide collectively, to produce and reproduce life without delegating it, to rebuild community ties, to recover knowledge, and to create spaces where human relations are not entirely determined by commodities and the state. This “concrete utopia” precisely expresses the desire not to postpone freedom until an uncertain future.




This demand strikes me as profoundly revolutionary. A revolution that doesn’t transform life would be a purely political revolution and, therefore, insufficient. We don’t want to change those who govern only to continue living under social relations we don’t control. We want the production, reproduction, and organisation of our existence to cease appearing to us as external powers. Emancipation cannot be reduced to modifying the administration of a society that remains essentially the same.




But precisely for this reason, I consider it necessary to raise a question that cannot be resolved by appealing solely to autonomy: What happens when an autonomous experience, even if real and transformative for those who participate in it, continues to develop within a capitalist society whose general relations remain intact?




An autonomous experience can profoundly transform the lives of those who participate in it and yet continue to exist within the market. It can create cooperative relationships and still need money; it can function without internal hierarchies and still have to buy goods produced by other workers; it can collectively organise a space and still remain subject to the property relations that govern the whole of society. It may even explicitly reject the logic of profit and yet depend, for its own reproduction, on an economy that remains dominated by that logic.




This does not prove that autonomous experiences are false or useless. It demonstrates something far more important: that an experience can begin to negate capitalism without yet having acquired the necessary strength to abolish it.




Herein lies the question I consider crucial. Autonomy is indispensable, but how can it cease to be a particular experience? How can it extend beyond a community, a territory, or a specific network of affinities? How can it confront a system that is not organised communally, but rather through general economic relations imposed on all its members, even against their will?




In other words, the fundamental question is not merely how to begin living differently, but 

which force can transform that possibility into a general transformation of society.




My answer to this question is the proletariat, because it is a class antagonistic to capital.




Hence, the question of revolution cannot be separated from a fundamental slogan: 

The self-organisation of the proletariat.

 It is not simply a matter of asserting that workers must emancipate themselves, but of arguing that they must organise their own struggle, their own decisions, and their own capacity to transform society. Autonomy then ceases to be a mere particular experience and acquires a class dimension: 

The proletariat must self-organise in order to cease being a force subordinate to capital and become a force capable of abolishing it.




The class struggle as a way of being in the world




There is also a difference in our political and intellectual background that helps to better understand our divergences. Miquel Amorós does not come from anarcho-syndicalism, although his thinking has frequently engaged with the history and experiences of the anarchist movement, but rather from Situationism and the various intellectual currents that followed the crisis and dissolution of that movement. His fundamental starting point lies in the critique of everyday life, alienation, technology, urbanism, and modern forms of domination, and from there he has developed a radical critique of industrial and capitalist society. In this evolution, the revolutionary centrality of the class struggle tends to be displaced in favour of other categories: Community, territory, autonomy, the defence of certain ways of life, or resistance against the multiple manifestations of domination.




My trajectory and my way of being in the world are different. Born in 1950 into a family of textile workers, the class struggle is not for me a choice or an intellectual preoccupation, nor is it an inherited theoretical category that can be replaced by another, as ideological or cultural fashions change. It is a lived reality, a way of understanding society 

and knowing

 one’s place within it. My priority has been, and continues to be, the class struggle and the emancipation of workers by the workers themselves. Not emancipation granted from above by the State, directed by a party, or administered by a bureaucracy, but the conscious self-emancipation of the proletariat through its own struggle and its own organisation. Elitist free islands, whether libertarian, liberal, or libertine, neither interest me nor are they part of my horizon.




And this is not workerism. I don’t idealise the worker, nor do I believe that being born into a working-class family confers any moral, political, or revolutionary superiority. Nor do I identify the proletariat with a specific working-class culture, the traditional factory, or an inherited identity. The centrality I grant to the proletariat doesn’t stem from nostalgia for the old working-class world or from defending a sociological identity. It arises from the recognition of a fundamental social reality: we live in a class-divided society, and as long as there are those who own the means of production and those who, in order to live, must sell their labour power, class antagonism will persist.




My way of being in the world is marked by this awareness. Not because workers are better than others, nor because they possess a moral superiority or an innate revolutionary virtue, but because their position in capitalist society places them in a specific relationship with capital. They are the ones who, through their daily activities, reproduce existing society and, precisely for that reason, are the ones who have the power to stop reproducing it and reorganise it on other foundations.




Class struggle is therefore not, for me, a theoretical preference among other possibilities, nor a category that can be abandoned when new forms of domination or new political sensibilities emerge. Capitalism has profoundly transformed the composition of the proletariat, dispersed its workplaces, fragmented its experiences, and multiplied the forms of exploitation and precarity. But it has not eliminated the fundamental separation between those who possess the material conditions of existence and those who must sell their labour power in order to live.




Perhaps this is one of the most profound differences between Amorós and myself. While his reflection, stemming from Situationism and its subsequent intellectual developments, tends to seek the possibilities of emancipation in the autonomy of ways of life, in community, in territory, and in resistance against the multiple manifestations of domination, I continue to believe that the core of all revolutionary possibility lies in the class struggle and in the emancipation of workers by the workers themselves.




Autonomy, community, and concrete experiences of liberation are indispensable. But they cannot replace the need for those who live by their labour to recognise themselves as a social force capable of transforming the entirety of existing relations. Defending this centrality does not mean worshipping the worker, but rather rejecting any emancipation granted from above and affirming that the liberation of the exploited can only be the conscious work of the exploited themselves.




It is not, therefore, a question of identity, nostalgia, or workerism. It is a way of being and existing in the world: Understanding that freedom cannot be granted, represented, or administered by others, and that the emancipation of workers will be the work of the workers themselves or it will not be.




The proletariat is not an identity, but a social relation.




To understand it, we must abandon an overly narrow view of the proletariat, such as Amorós’s. The proletariat is not simply the industrial worker in the large factory, nor a particular working-class culture, nor a political identity inherited from the 19

th

 or 20

th

-century labour movement. It is a class defined by a social relation: That of those who, being separated from the means necessary to autonomously produce their existence, must sell their labour power to capital in order to live.




This definition is crucial because it allows us to understand why the proletariat occupies a position that no other social category can replace. The worker does not simply stand before capital as a victim of an external power. Their own labour power constitutes one of the conditions for the reproduction of capital. Capital buys this labour power because it needs to use it in the production process and obtain from it a value greater than what it has paid. Without wage labour, there is no valorisation of capital; and without valorisation, there is no reproduction of capital as a social relation.




The relationship between capital and the proletariat thus contains a contradiction that cannot be resolved through reforms or the mere creation of alternative spaces. Capital needs the proletariat to reproduce itself, while the proletariat can only emancipate itself by ceasing to reproduce capital. This contradiction explains the revolutionary centrality of the proletariat in a far more compelling way than any moral, historical, or identity-based consideration.




The proletariat is not the protagonist of the revolution because it is «the poorest», nor because it possesses a supposed ethical superiority, nor because a political tradition has decided to assign it that role. It is the protagonist because it occupies a unique material position within the capitalist structure: 

It produces that which allows capital to valorise itself and, precisely for this reason, can interrupt the valorisation process and begin to destroy the relationship that sustains it.




Herein lies the fundamental difference. A community can resist capital, but it does not, in itself, constitute the relationship that allows capital to reproduce itself. A territory can defend itself against capital, but it does not necessarily contain the antagonism capable of abolishing the wage relationship. A cooperative can organise an economic activity differently and still continue to function within the market. A self-managed experiment can demonstrate that it is possible to collectively organise certain tasks and, at the same time, be forced to reproduce economic relations that exist outside of it.




The proletariat, on the other hand, is at the very heart of the valorisation process. Therefore, their action can have a consequence that no isolated experience can produce: The interruption of the social reproduction of capital.




The revolution is not about managing capital differently.




This point also helps us understand what proletarian emancipation truly means. The proletariat is not called upon to seize power in order to manage capitalist society from a new position. A revolution that replaced private owners with a state or bureaucratic administration would have changed the form of ownership without necessarily abolishing the social relations that make capital possible.




Proletarian emancipation is more radical. The proletariat cannot liberate itself simply by becoming the collective owners of businesses, because that would preserve fundamental forms of separation between producers and the social conditions of production. Nor can it limit itself to improving the conditions of wage labour, because wages themselves presuppose the separation that constitutes the worker as a proletarian.




The revolutionary goal, therefore, is not for the proletariat to find a better place within capitalist society. Its goal is for it to cease to exist as a proletariat through the abolition of the social relations that constitute it as such.




This is why proletarian protagonism does not lead to a new class society, but rather to the possibility of abolishing classes altogether. The working class does not emancipate itself to become the ruling class. It emancipates itself by destroying the conditions that make the existence of ruling and dominated classes possible. Therein lies the universal character of its struggle.




The transformation of the proletariat does not mean its disappearance




It could be objected that all of this pertains to a class composition that no longer exists. Indeed, the contemporary proletariat does not present the same forms it had in other eras. But to confuse the historical transformation of the proletariat with its disappearance would mean accepting precisely the superficial definition that should be rejected.




Capitalism has fragmented labour, shifted production to a global scale, multiplied forms of employment, and extended precariousness. The contemporary worker can be found in a factory, a hospital, a hotel, a logistics warehouse, a digital platform, an office, a farm, or in the care economy. The traditional boundaries between production and reproduction have become much more complex.




But none of these transformations eliminates the fundamental relationship of those who need to sell their labour power to reproduce their existence. The class has changed its composition because capitalism has changed; it has not disappeared because its composition has changed.




Precisely because capitalism has dispersed the proletariat, the political question is to rebuild its unity based on what it has in common, not to replace it with a vaguer category. This is especially important in an era when the fragmentation of social experiences can give the impression that there is no longer a subject capable of acting upon the whole.




The revolutionary problem of our time is not to find a new identity to replace the proletariat. It is 

to find the proletariat where capitalism has dispersed it.




Community cannot take the place of class.




Community can be an extraordinarily important space of resistance. It can protect needs that the market destroys, rebuild bonds that competition dissolves, and produce concrete experiences of cooperation. It can even become a privileged terrain for revolutionary organisation.




But community and class are not equivalent concepts.




A territorial community can bring together people subjected to different social relations. It can include workers and owners, wage earners and rentiers, exploited people and people who benefit from certain forms of ownership. They can unite against a specific enemy and yet separate when the question of ownership or the appropriation of wealth arises.




Therefore, territorial struggles can be contemporary expressions of the class struggle without territory becoming the new universal subject. The issue is not to deny these struggles, but to understand when and how they express class antagonism and how they can be integrated into a struggle capable of challenging capitalist relations as a whole. The same applies to ecology, housing, care work, and territorial defence. Capitalism permeates all these dimensions of existence, and for that very reason, they are fundamental arenas for contemporary proletarian struggle. But they remain intertwined with class. The issue is not finding a new subject to replace the proletariat, but rather recognising the proletariat wherever capitalism has extended and transformed its forms of exploitation.




Autonomy needs a force capable of generalising it.




Herein lies the point where the question of the proletariat acquires its full importance. Autonomy is not the problem; the problem is its limits when it remains isolated.




If an autonomous experience remains separate, capitalism can surround it, condition it, absorb it, or simply wait for its exhaustion. If it manages to spread, the question of its coordination and its confrontation with general social relations immediately arises. At that point, it is no longer enough to speak of community: The need for a force capable of intervening in social reproduction emerges.




The revolution cannot consist of endlessly multiplying small exceptions to capitalism. It must transform these exceptions into a new and general form of the reproduction of life. To do this, it is necessary to appropriate what is currently organised by capital: workplaces, the means of production, distribution networks, infrastructure, urban spaces, and, ultimately, the material conditions of existence.




This appropriation cannot be carried out by an isolated community. Only a class that, by virtue of its position in the production process, has the capacity to halt and reorganise that process can achieve this. At this point, autonomy ceases to be merely a mode of organisation and becomes a question of social power: Who has the effective capacity to stop the functioning of capitalist society and set in motion another form of life reproduction? The answer remains the proletariat.




The question of parliamentarism




Parliamentarism occupies a much smaller place in this difference than is sometimes claimed. We are both anti-parliamentarian, but we don’t understand exactly what needs to be overcome when parliamentarism is rejected: Amorós insists more on the incompatibility between emancipation and institutional representation, while I link this critique to a broader issue: The autonomy of the proletarian movement in the face of any form of separate power and the need for decisions to remain in the hands of those directly involved in the struggle.




Therefore, the problem is not simply refusing to participate in Parliament. The problem is preventing the separation between those who struggle and those who speak on their behalf from recurring. And this question only acquires its full meaning when it is linked to the central problem: Which class should retain in its own hands the capacity to decide on its struggle and on the transformation of society.




1936: When autonomy ceased to be an idea




The Spanish revolutionary experience allows us to understand this issue concretely. In 1936, the workers did not wait for any institution to recognise their right to transform society. They created their own organisations, occupied factories and land, organised militias and collectives, and effectively altered power relations. This was much more than a communal experience: It was a proletarian uprising capable of profoundly altering the existing social reproduction.




But that experience also revealed the decisive difficulty: As long as state structures capable of regaining authority existed, and as long as revolutionary organisations could not impose autonomous social coordination against them, the gains could be contained and ultimately defeated. The events of May 1937 constituted a brutal expression of this contradiction.




The lesson is not to claim that the collectives were a mistake. It is to understand that they were insufficient because their social force did not become widespread enough to destroy the relations that could return power to the State and capital.




This is a fundamental difference. Revolutionary autonomy does not fail because it is too autonomous; it fails when it cannot become a sufficiently broad social force to prevent the reconstruction of what it seeks to abolish. And this problem brings us back to the proletariat.




Here, therefore, appears the slogan that summarises the fundamental political problem: 

The self-organisation of the proletariat.

 If capitalism has fragmented the workers, dispersed their experiences, and weakened their traditional forms of organisation, the task is not to wait for an institution to once again represent their unity. Nor is it to replace the proletariat with a sum of particular communities, movements, or identities. The task is for the proletarians themselves to rebuild their capacity to recognise, deliberate, decide, and act collectively.




Self-organisation

 means precisely that the organisation of the struggle cannot be separated from those who struggle. It means that decisions remain in the hands of the workers and that no external leadership can appropriate their power, speak permanently on their behalf, or replace their initiative. But it also means something more: That organisation is not an external instrument simply intended to achieve reforms, but rather the process by which the proletariat begins to recognise itself as a common social force, capable of halting the reproduction of capital and reorganising life on other foundations.




Therefore, the slogan cannot simply be “autonomy,” but rather 

the self-organisation of the proletariat.

 Autonomy signifies the need for independence from the state, political parties, integrated trade unions, and all forms of separate power; self-organisation indicates 

who

 should exercise that autonomy and 

how

 it can become an effective historical force. The crucial issue is that those who produce and reproduce capitalist society must learn to organise themselves in order to cease reproducing it.




Autonomy as a form of proletarian revolution




From this perspective, defending the proletariat does not mean abandoning autonomy, but rather giving it concrete social content. Autonomy means that the class organises itself and that no institution, party, union, or external leadership can replace it. It does not mean building a sphere separate from capitalism, but rather acquiring the capacity to confront it and transform the relations that organise society.




Therefore, it also does not mean living indefinitely in small, alternative spaces. It means beginning to build, from concrete struggles, a different form of social reproduction. And it does not mean replacing the State with an organisation that governs in the name of the workers, but rather preventing the re-emergence of a separation between those who decide and those who obey.




The proletariat is the protagonist of the revolution precisely when it ceases to be understood as a passive sociological category and begins to act as a social force conscious of its position. It is a class that produces, transports, cares, builds, cleans, cultivates, distributes, and maintains the infrastructure and services upon which society depends. It does so, however, under conditions determined by capital. This position constitutes its weakness as long as it remains subordinate, but this is also its historical strength, because those who participate decisively in the material reproduction of society possess the power to disrupt and reorganise it.




The bourgeoisie possesses capital, and the state has coercion at its disposal, but neither can replace the activity of the proletariat. When this activity ceases to be subordinate to capital, the material foundation of existing society begins to disappear.




Revolutionary optimism




Defending proletarian leadership today should not be a defensive stance, a nostalgic exercise, or a ritualistic repetition of old formulas. On the contrary, it is a profoundly optimistic affirmation. It means recognising that capitalism is not an invulnerable whole and that society is not condemned to reproduce itself eternally under the same relations. It means understanding that the force that keeps this society functioning is also the force that can stop it.




We don’t need to invent the subject of revolution from the outside. That subject already exists. It exists wherever someone has to sell their labour power to live; it exists wherever an activity necessary for society is subordinated to the production of value; it exists in the factory and the hospital, in the hotel and the logistics warehouse, in the countryside, in transportation, on the digital platform, and in care work. It exists wherever capital needs labour to reproduce itself.




What still doesn’t exist to the necessary degree is the awareness of that force, its autonomous organisation, and its capacity to recognise itself as a common force. That is the fundamental political problem of our time.




The issue, therefore, is not abandoning concrete utopia, but preventing concrete utopia from becoming a substitute for revolution. It is not a matter of choosing between living now and transforming the world, but of transforming the world so that what we can only experience today as an exception can become the common condition for all.




The proletariat and the possibility of revolution




This is, ultimately, the reason why I defend the proletarian leading role in the revolution. Not because all other struggles are unimportant, nor because the entire working class automatically acts in a revolutionary manner, nor because the proletariat possesses an innate revolutionary consciousness, and certainly not because one must uphold a promise out of fidelity to tradition. I defend it because its position within capitalism contains a possibility that no other social position contains in the same way: 

The possibility of abolishing the relationship upon which the reproduction of capital depends.




Capital has done everything possible to fragment the proletariat, to individualise it, to make it precarious, to pit it against itself, and to convince each worker that they exist solely as an individual competing with others for survival. But this fragmentation has not destroyed the social relationship that binds them together. Wherever there is wage labour, wherever life depends on selling one’s labour power, wherever capital needs to appropriate the labour of others to increase its value, antagonism still exists.




The revolutionary task is not to invent something else to replace it. It is to make conscious, organised, and effective the force that already exists. Therefore, the revolutionary horizon is not a community that has managed to escape the world, but a world from which escape is no longer necessary. We do not want to conquer a corner of freedom while the rest of society remains subjugated. We want freedom to cease being the privilege of those who have managed to build a protected space and to become the material condition of everyone.




We do not wait for a historical saviour to appear. We do not wait for a vanguard to think for us. We do not wait for the State to grant us freedom. The force capable of radically transforming the world already exists within it: It is the force of those who, working every day to reproduce capitalist society, can one day decide to stop reproducing it.




The revolution begins when the proletariat understands that it is not condemned to be the labour force of capital, but that it can become the social force capable of abolishing it. Then the struggle ceases to be a desperate defence against advancing barbarism and becomes a conscious offensive for human emancipation. It is no longer a question of conquering a more dignified place within a world that condemns us to exploitation, but of ending the social relations that make exploitation possible; it is no longer a question of preserving a few spaces of freedom within existing society, but of making freedom the foundation of all society.




Because this is, ultimately, the question before us: 

Either capital leads humanity toward ever-deepening barbarism, or the proletariat finds in its own strength the capacity to stop it and pave the way for a world without classes, without exploitation and domination, without police, without armies, without borders, without states.




The revolution will not be the administration of an inherited world, but its conscious abolition to make another possible. The slogan that emerges from all of the above is, therefore, simple and at the same time decisive: 

the self-organisation of the proletariat.

 We do not expect anyone to organise from the outside the force capable of emancipating us. We do not expect an institution to represent us, a vanguard to think for us, or a State to transform existing social relations from above.




Revolutionary organisation can only arise from the struggle itself, from the capacity of the exploited to recognise themselves as a common force and to take into their own hands the decisions that affect their existence. 

Self-organisation

 does not mean confining oneself to a working-class identity or building an organisation separate from society; 

it means collectively organising the force of those who live by their labour to abolish the social relations that make them proletarians.




Therefore, in the face of fragmentation, representation, and delegation, the slogan remains: 

self-organisation of the proletariat.

 Not as an empty formula, but as the concrete process by which the class that reproduces the world of capital today can begin to organise its abolition.




And this time we will not fight to conquer the future: We will fight so that, at last, the future ceases to belong to capital and belongs to emancipated humanity.
