title: The General Strike in Spain on November 11th
content:
The 24-hour general strike that took place on Wednesday, November 11

th

, involving around 4 million people, had its origins in the big protests in October against the housing policies of the Socialist Party (PSOE) government, led by Pedro Sanchez, in alliance with the left Movimiento Sumar, especially against the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal which eventually led to her death.  Rents have risen by 45% and house prices by 68%. Between 2008 and 2015 there were 500,000 evictions. These protests themselves involved millions turning out in many parts of Spain.




Sanchez responded by dissolving his government and calling for snap elections on November 29

th

. He hoped to blackmail the movement by offering a false alternative of supporting the PSOE government, or opening the way to a government of the Popular Party-PP (with its roots in Francoism) and the fascist Vox party.




A movement towards organising a general strike began with the housing movement, especially around the Sindicato de Inquilinas e Inquilinos (Tenants Union) of Madrid, spreading to Catalonia. It coordinated with the syndicalist and anarcho-syndicalist unions CGT and CNT (100,000 members and 15,000 members respectively. These jointly organised neighbourhood strike committees, which ensured massive strike pickets on the day.




The leadership of the union centrals UGT, controlled by the PSOE, and in alliance with Sumar, and the CCOO, controlled by the Stalinists, then were forced to swing in behind the strike call, hoping to gain control of the movement.




This is in the context not just of the housing crisis, but of wages remaining stagnant, and rising inflation. The cost of living has shot up considerably, by at least 45%, with big food, and energy increases. In the meantime, corporate profits have risen 40%.




Sanchez used the vote in Congress (Parliament), where a Housing Decree, reforms announced to head off the housing movement, was blocked by the PP, Vox, and the Catalan right-wing party Junts. The PSOE was re-elected in 2023, on a promise to halt the housing crisis. A huge building boom led to a slump, but instead of socialising the huge number of empty houses, the PSOE government sold them cheaply to investment bankers. Promised rent controls and increases in social housing were not enacted, whilst tax breaks were given to the big landlords.




The Sanchez government and its allies in the UGT and CCOO leadership hoped to use the mobilisation to stay in power. However, the four million who turned out on the day, are acting against the policies of the PSOE-Sumar government, disgusted by both the crises in housing and the cost of living. On the day, the various unions influenced by anarchism and anarcho-syndicalism mobilised their members, as did the many neighbourhood housing action committees, which have a membership of 10,000.




Despite the bad weather in some regions, there were massive demonstrations and large blockades in many towns and cities. The biggest was in Madrid, despite teeming rain, followed by that in Barcelona. The strike began at midnight. Blockades were put up on major highways, and large workplaces were picketed. Strikes heavily impacted industries in Madrid, Catalonia, Valencia, and the Basque country, and less so in other cities and provinces.




The railways were completely closed down, with a strike beginning the day before. Big chain stores were picketed and shut down, including supermarkets like Mercadona, Adidas, Benetton, El Cortes Ingles and Zara.




Of course, the forces of the State intervened, with the cops attacking demonstrations and making at least 115 arrests.




On the day after the mobilisation, Sanchez introduced another two decrees that were almost identical to the rejected ones. They were presented to a smaller parliamentary council on Thursday, giving the government a better chance of passing the laws. The first decree passed narrowly and includes a measure extending protections against evictions for tenants deemed by social services to be in a precarious financial or social position, as long as regional authorities cannot offer them an alternative residence. Another measure attempted to reduce real estate speculation by stopping any company involved in the real estate market from buying properties for less than 70 percent of their value.




However, it was rejected. again narrowly, after the centre-right Basque party voted with the right-wing bloc after having supported the other decree. The PP and Vox pledged to repeal these reforms if they come to power on November 29

th

. These reforms have only limited effect, as the central government has no direct power over the regional autonomous governments on housing policies, which control regulation and planning, public housing and rental markets.




The November 11

th

 general strike was massive. But one day is not enough. Already there is an awareness that further future mobilisations are needed, and further protests are being planned by the housing unions, the CGT, CNT, the assembly’s union Intersindical Alternativa de Catalunya (IAC), and the Basque unions, ELA and LAB, to pressurise the big landlords and the regional governments.




The Spanish working class is increasingly disenchanted with the ploys of the PSOE government and its left allies, whilst rejecting the PP and Vox. It must now look urgently to creating its own autonomous organisations in both workplace and neighbourhood, independent of the political parties and looking towards building its own strength, and in the long term, looking towards the coming about of libertarian communism, postponed in 1937.

author: ACG
title: Resistance to Data Centres in Ireland
content:
From a correspondent  in the Republic of Ireland.




On November 7

th 

over 2,000 participated in a protest march in Dublin. The action was against data centres. There was a range of ages and organisations represented, from children to grandparents, environmental and community groups as well as political parties.  It was part of a co-ordinated Europe-wide response to a growing problem.




There are a number of reasons to oppose data centres and those at the protest voiced a variety of objections. One of the most commonly expressed complaints is their massive consumption of energy, often 24 hours a day. They compete with houses, schools and hospitals in this regard and the figures for the past decade show the increase they have made in consumption.




In the case of Ireland the Central Statistics Office (CSO) shows that data centres accounted for just 5% of consumption in 2015, but this had skyrocketed to 23% in 2025 (CSO.ie). This resulted in Irish households paying an estimated 715 Euros more in electricity bills from 2015 to 2023. This trend is likely to continue under current conditions. Campaign group Friends of the Earth predicts in a report that if that is the case, costs on households could mean an additional 1.43 billion Euros in electricity bills by 2034 (friendsoftheearth.ie).




oplus_32




Environmental concern can be found in their use of water. Data centres use huge amounts for their cooling systems. This puts pressure on local water supplies, especially during periods of drought or water restrictions. This is not a purely theoretical point in the case of Ireland. An indication of the general governmental attitude towards water usage can been seen in this year’s 2 and a half month ban on the use of hosepipes during summer. This was applied in Dublin and a number of other areas. However, an exemption was made for business during the ban (RTE, 22nd July 2026).




To put water use in perspective, total data centre water usage in Ireland was around 1 billion litres in 2025. Academics from universities in Ireland and Catalonia estimated in a recent joint report that this was equivalent to 18.5% of the consumption of occupied households in the Republic during that period (Irish Times 24/9/26). Over 95% of this water was consumed by the Mark Zuckerberg controlled Meta (Facebook, Whatsapp) alone.




Another reason sometimes forwarded in favour of data centres is the job creation that supposedly results. Its true they may employ workers during the construction phase of a project, but once up and running, data centres don’t need many people on an ongoing basis. Even those who remain once a data centre is established, don’t stay in the jobs very long. Data centre operations in Europe and Ireland show a low employee retention rate paired with a relatively short median tenure of 1.8 years. Linkedin data shows a high job turnover, with a minimum of 1,100 professionals changing jobs in a year (Savillis.ie). There is also the increase in AI services, which data centres’ enable. This deskills labour and puts human jobs at risk.




oplus_32




A further concern is the way the data centres are tied-in to the military-industrial complex. The ones in Ireland operated by Google, Microsoft and Amazon host cloud and AI infrastructure that support digital economies and military-connected cloud systems (KPMG.com). Human rights organisations such as the Irish Council for Civil Liberties have raised complaints about this, including the fact that Irish-based storage of data is tied to military and surveillance operations linked to foreign occupations and wars (ICCL.ie). Officially the Irish state claims to be neutral, but ever since World War 2, this has been more a form of neutrality that leans towards certain powers rather than others. The updating of technology is therefore really a continuation of a long-standing approach to intelligence gathering and geopolitics.




Data centres are clearly problematic. Those who have joined the opposition to them hold a combination of motivations, as can be seen in the broad demographics and organisational diversity of those who took part in the recent demonstrations. Along with this multiplicity of people, there is a variety of tactics that can be applied to the issue. At one end of the spectrum, there is the signing of a petition or marches like the ones held in Dublin. A march has its place. It at least raises greater awareness that a problem exists. The difficulty is often that petitions and marches ultimately only reinforce people’s sense of passivity, since they entail appealing to politicians to fix the very ill they created in the first place.




Further along the continuum is a perspective that argues ordinary people should directly own and control resources in society. Existing community-based groups certainly have the potential kernel of this view within them. This is something that should be encouraged. With ownership and self-management of what is produced, we can decide if we want data centres, where, when and how. In such circumstances the environment we are all part of will not be put under strain, workers and communities will decide what work needs to be done and whether we really want to support the mass killing of ordinary people elsewhere.




As for tactics, direct action is a more empowering approach. This is one where we intervene directly to change a particular situation. Instead of asking others to fix something for us, we do it ourselves here and now. There is not much sign of such activity in Ireland to be honest, but it has happened elsewhere in relation to data centres. As part of the same weekend of continent-wide initiatives, activists from the direct action group Geef Tegangas physically occupied a Microsoft data centre in Westpoort, Amsterdam. They drew attention to the use of its services by the Israeli military and Trump’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency (The Guardian 6/11/26). It’s a small contribution compared to the much bigger series of actions required to achieve deeper change, but it does point to a method and aim that is likely to be more effective in the long run.




To sum up, the march in Dublin was a small component of a much larger move to oppose data centres. Due to the complex mix of participants, motivations and tactics of the wider movement, we can say it should be supported, but with a critical eye towards some aspects of what is happening. Get involved if you can.

title: Labour and the budget: same old same old (with a side of pickles)
content:
When Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey presented his budget on Wednesday October 28

th

 he said: “This is a Budget for the working people of Britain. For British businesses, big and small.”  Well, no. It offered little to working people, and plenty to businesses, to the military and to the defence industry.




We were offered the pittance of 86p a week off of electricity bills. In addition, there will be a £100 one-off winter fuel payment for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D. This will almost immediately be wiped out by a predicted rise by £276 in January, to just under £2,000 a year. Another forecast from the EDF energy company, predicted that it might rise higher than this.




Healey introduced a £2 cap on single bus fares in England from January 2027. But, for example, many workers and students in London cannot afford to live in inner London and must make long journeys by bus to get to work and study, because they cannot afford the rail and tube fares.




He also announced the end of gas standing charges, which will save a mere £45 a year, and then only for 60% of households. Healey had already announced that an extra £432 million would be spent on a programme to get rough sleepers in England off the streets. title: SOLIDARITY WITH ALL ANTI-WAR PRISONERS IN RUSSIA & DRAFT DODGERS IN UKRAINE
content:
Beneath is the text of the leaflet distributed outside both the Russian and Ukrainian embassies in London by members of the Anarchist Communist Group and the Network of Anarchist Internationalists (NAI) on Saturday October 31st







For the past five years, the warring states of Ukraine and Russia have been sending the working class to die on the battlefields, killing civilians across the war zone and destroying critical infrastructure with missiles and drones. European states are arming Ukraine, helping to keep the war of the trenches going on indefinitely—a war that has already lasted longer than WWI—in order to lay the groundwork for the revitalisation of their declining industry by shifting it more and more toward a war economy. The endless war, financed by loans from Europe and the USA, allows states to carry out their ideological, bureaucratic and technical “defensive” restructuring, as well as the broader restructuring of production, at a time when the US is pulling back from funding the war in the region and the whole planet is beginning to smell of gunpowder. The loans under the Rearm Europe arms program and the record ‘defence’ budgets being pushed by Europe point with certainty toward war austerity, in other words an even harsher exploitation of the working class, as its future wages are put up as collateral for current spending.
